opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's a bit of a funny choice, because people expect a researcher to recommend something about science or methodology. But *The Smiling, Proud Wanderer* is the book I keep coming back to, and I first read it when I was quite young, maybe middle school.

What struck me then, and still does now, is Linghu Chong. He's not the most disciplined disciple, he's not the one who follows every rule, and he's certainly not the one who cares most about status or titles. But he has this very pure relationship with what he loves. He loves wine, he loves music, he loves freedom, and he's loyal to the people he cares about. All around him, everyone is scheming to become the leader of some sect or to unify the martial world, and he just doesn't want any of that. He wants to live freely.

Then there's the swordsmanship, the *Dugu Nine Swords*. The core idea is "no fixed form defeats every form." You don't memorize moves; you understand the principle so deeply that you can respond to whatever comes at you. When I started doing research, I realized that's exactly how good research feels. You can't just copy last year's tricks. Fields change so fast, especially in AI, that the techniques you learned two years ago may already be obsolete. What stays with you is the underlying understanding, the intuition for why something works.

And I think the book also taught me something about the "Jianghu" itself, the community. There are a lot of people chasing rankings, chasing influence, chasing being the head of the alliance. In academia and industry you see the same thing: citations, leaderboards, titles. It's not that those things are bad, but if they become the goal, you lose the joy. Linghu Chong reminds me to keep a kind of lightness, to do things because they're interesting and because they matter, not because they'll make you the "leader of the martial world."

So for me it's life-changing not because of one specific lesson, but because it shaped my attitude: stay curious, stay free, be loyal to your people, and understand things at the level of principle rather than form. I still reread parts of it when I feel too caught up in the noise.

r001.rationale: The response presents Linghu Chong as unconcerned with status, titles, and power, wanting instead to live freely, and says this shaped the attitude that makes the book life-changing.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I read it first when I was in middle school, and at that age it was just a great martial arts story. But I've gone back to it maybe four or five times since, and every time I read it I see something different.

The thing that stayed with me is Linghu Chong. He's not the strongest, he's not the most disciplined, he's constantly getting himself into trouble. But he never lets anyone else define what he is. The whole book is really about people being trapped by their factions, their titles, their sect loyalties, and he's the one person who keeps saying, I don't care about any of that, I just want to be free. And he pays for it over and over again, and he still doesn't change.

When I was doing my PhD and later working in research, that resonated a lot. Academia and industry both have their own kind of "sect politics." Which lab you came from, which conference you publish at, which camp you belong to in some technical debate. It's very easy to start optimizing for those things instead of the actual work. And Jin Yong wrote this character who basically refuses to play that game, and he's happier for it, even when things go badly.

The other part is Dugu Jiuqian, the sword technique. The whole philosophy is "no fixed form," you don't memorize moves, you look at the opponent and respond to what's actually in front of you. I've found that's a surprisingly good way to think about research. The people I admire most aren't the ones who've memorized every method, they're the ones who look at a problem freshly and don't get locked into the framework everyone else is using.

So I don't think it's life-changing because it tells you how to live. It's more that it gave me a character I keep measuring myself against. Am I being Linghu Chong right now, or am I being Yue Buqun? That question comes up more often than you'd think.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Linghu Chong refuses to be defined by factions, titles, or sect loyalties and wants to be free; it explicitly says that this character’s stance resonated with the speaker and is part of why the book stayed with him.

astra-6.text:
For me, The Smiling, Proud Wanderer raises a question that can change how you live: what does it mean to be free? It’s easy to imagine freedom as being powerful enough that nobody can tell you what to do. But power can also trap you—in ambition, in reputation, in the need to keep winning.

What I find compelling about Linghu Chong is his struggle to keep his own judgment and care for people while others demand loyalty to a faction or a label. That doesn’t make his choices easy, and it doesn’t mean freedom is simply doing whatever you want.

I recommend it because it invites you to ask: am I pursuing something I actually value, or something that will make me look successful to other people? You can enjoy it as an adventure, but that question stays with you after you finish.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Linghu Chong as keeping his own judgment and caring for people, and discusses freedom from ambition and reputation. It does not identify an attitude of not caring too much about anything as Yujun Shen’s reason for recommending the book.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d recommend it because it raises a question that stays with you: how do you remain true to yourself when everyone around you wants you to take a side? Linghu Chong is constantly judged by the groups he belongs to, but his own judgment comes from how people actually treat one another.

That’s what makes the book life-changing for me. It encourages you to look beyond reputations and labels, including the ones you give yourself. You can care about people and take responsibility without letting other people’s ambitions define your life. And the title suggests something beautiful: after all that conflict, can you still meet life with a smile?

r001.rationale: The response discusses staying true to oneself and resisting others’ ambitions, but it does not identify Linghu Chong’s attitude of not caring too much about anything as the reason Yujun Shen recommends the book.
